blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define living standards, set out the indicators that measure them, and see why one money figure alone may mislead.

blocks.heading: Living standards and the indicators that measure them
blocks.text:
Living standards are the level of material well-being of a person or a household: how well the household is housed, fed, clothed, schooled and cared for, together with the security of that level. The starting measure is Gross Domestic Product - the total value of the goods and services produced in a country in a given period - but for living standards the figure to use is GDP per head, that total divided by the population: it shows the average output available per person, so countries of different sizes compare.

The indicators that complete the picture: income per person; health measures such as life expectancy and infant mortality; education measures such as mean years of schooling and literacy; and access to basic services such as clean water and electricity. Together they capture what GDP per head alone may miss, and they travel in company: where output per person rises, health and schooling tend to rise with it.

blocks.heading: Reading the figures for two countries
blocks.text: Namibia records GDP of N$150 billion and a population of 2.5 million: GDP per head is N$150 000m / 2.5m, which is N$60 000 a year. Vietnam, as a non-African example, records GDP of US$300 billion with 100 million people: GDP per head is US$3 000 a year, and at N$20 to US$1 that is N$60 000 as well, so the averages match. The other indicators: life expectancy 74 years in Vietnam against 60 in Namibia, household electricity 99% against about half. One figure is a doorway, not a verdict: the same GDP per head stands while health and access separate the two, because GDP per head is an average that may hide how income is shared.

blocks.heading: What GDP per head may hide
blocks.text: GDP per head is an average, so where income is spread unevenly the typical household may earn well below it: a mean of N$60 000 can stand beside a majority earning a fraction of that. Output may also include goods that change living standards little, so the health and access indicators travel further than the money figure.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The national income behind these figures is built in topic 4.1, price changes that distort comparisons belong to topic 4.2, and the sharing of income follows here.
